doc.title: Frank Foster and Bill Hughes interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, Schenectady, New York, March 28, 1995

chapter: The late-1950s Basie band and closing
title: The great late-1950s Basie band
summary: Foster and Hughes praise Sonny Payne, lead players and the rhythm section as the New Testament band.

story.theme_name: Playing with Count Basie: joining, leading, leaving
story.community_name: Playing with Count Basie: the band, its feel and its people

blocks.x: Yeah. And I don’t know, it was just a feeling, especially for me, that Sonny Payne hit the thing right on the head that we needed right at that point. More so than Joe Williams to me. Although it really didn’t ring into me on Joe Williams until I heard those records being played all over the place. But Sonny, like he had a knack for moving this band at that time.

You know the thing with the juggling the sticks, throwing the sticks up and catching them and hitting right on a given beat, and this was, when you catch an audience with a visual extravaganza as well as a aural or musical—
And there we were, two of the, you know—

And Joe and Sonny were two of the most colorful characters in the band, which was full of colorful characters. Everybody had a story. And then when we acquired the likes of Snooky Young to play lead trumpet, and there was Joe Newman and —
I think that was the final piece when Snooky was —

That was the icing on the cake. And that was arguably the greatest of all Basie bands. That was the New Testament band. The Old Testament band being the band from the late 30’s and early 40’s. In the late 40’s it wasn’t such, it was good but it wasn’t—
It wasn’t as polished as the band in the late 50’s.

Right. We developed into a precision, a slick, precision, east coast jazz machine. But still, lots of feeling, the feeling never left. So the precision and the polish came, and the feeling, you know it just steamrolled over people. And with Joe Williams and Sonny Payne there too, and Marshall Royal playing lead alto, I mean he was, see the voice of the band was Marshall Royal, Snooky Young and Henry Coker, the lead players. And together they gave the band one hell-fired voice.
Yes they did. You’re making me cry for it.

And then the Freddie Green metronomic but still loose, happy rhythm, and Eddie Jones, who acquired a technique of walking the bass that was just phenomenal. And then Sonny Payne with the power that he gave to it. The All American Rhythm Section of the late 50’s. And hey—
It was a great time to be alive.
It really was. And a great time to be young, you know, like I was in my early 20’s, from 24 until about 32 years of age. That was right in the meat of party time.

You know when you tend to think of old time bands as being old musicians, you know. But what was really happening was that these bands were young bands.
